response.passage: Rohan visited a shop to buy a new cricket bat marked at ₹2,000. The shopkeeper offered a 10% discount on the marked price. To find the discount amount, we calculate 10% of ₹2,000, which is ₹200. Thus, the selling price becomes ₹1,800. Rohan decided to sell his old bat for ₹500, which he had originally bought for ₹400. Since the selling price is higher than the cost price, he made a profit of ₹100. He calculated his profit percentage by dividing the profit by the cost price, resulting in 25%. Later, Rohan invested ₹1,000 in a bank at a simple interest rate of 10% per annum for 6 months. To calculate the interest, he converted 6 months into 0.5 years. Using the formula (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100, he found the interest to be ₹50. Finally, he considered a scheme offering two successive discounts of 10% and 20%. He correctly calculated that this is not a flat 30% discount, because the second discount is applied only to the already reduced price. By applying these methods, Rohan avoided common mistakes and managed his finances effectively.
response.summary: This passage explains how to correctly calculate discounts based on marked prices and profit percentages based on cost prices. It also demonstrates the importance of using consistent time units for interest calculations and explains why successive discounts are not additive.
